title: Scientist Claims He Can Cure Aging in 3 Years
summary: At age 10, William "Bill" Andrews had a conversation with his father that changed his life. "Living is the greatest thing that ever happened to us," his father said. "When you grow up, you should become a doctor and find a cure for aging." From then on, Andrews had one mission. Now 74, Andrews is a practicing molecular biologist with a PhD. He claims he's on the brink of creating an anti-aging pill for the masses. He says all he needs is funding to scale it. Andrews's approach focuses on telomeres—tiny protectors at the ends of chromosomes, our packages of DNA. Think of them like the plastic tips on shoelaces. Over time, they wear down, and cells stop dividing. That's aging. But an enzyme called telomerase can rebuild telomeres, essentially hitting a reset button. The catch: telomerase is only consistently active in reproductive cells, stem cells, and cancer cells. Most other cells are designed to age and die to protect the body from uncontrolled growth. Andrews wants to find a gene that can switch on telomerase production in all cells. "I was searching for molecules that, when added to human cells and petri dishes, would turn the telomerase gene on," he says. He argues that aging is no longer necessary for humans. "Our species isn't at risk of collapsing if your grandmother lives to 150," he says. He believes we can overcome overpopulation issues. His main goal is to stop suffering from age-related diseases like cancer, heart disease, and dementia. In 2009, scientists won a Nobel Prize for discovering telomerase, which became the foundation for Andrews's work. While some may be skeptical, Andrews is determined. "It will make us younger in every way imaginable—make us look, feel, and behave like we're 25 again," he claims. If his research succeeds, Andrews believes the pill could change how we think about growing older—turning aging from an unavoidable fact of life into a problem science can solve.
why_it_matters: Populations almost everywhere are ageing, which strains health systems and pension budgets, so a genuine anti-aging treatment would reshape economies and families — but it also raises hard questions about who could afford it, and whether a claim announced before peer-reviewed proof deserves the same trust as a tested medicine.

questions.question: What did scientists win a Nobel Prize for in 2009?

background_read: Andrews's claim sits inside a fast-growing research field often called geroscience — the study of why bodies age and whether the process can be slowed. The Nobel Prize he builds on was awarded in 2009 to Elizabeth Blackburn, Carol Greider and Jack Szostak for discovering how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and by the enzyme telomerase.

That discovery came with a warning, though. Blackburn has publicly cautioned that telomerase is not a simple anti-aging switch: most human cancers keep telomerase switched on so they can divide endlessly, which is one reason the body restricts it to a few cell types. The wear-down Andrews wants to reverse is known as the 'Hayflick limit', named after Leonard Hayflick, who showed in the 1960s that ordinary human cells divide only a limited number of times before stopping.

Andrews is a real figure in the field — he ran a biotech company called Sierra Sciences that searched for ways to activate telomerase — but his approach competes with other strategies, such as calorie restriction, drugs that clear out worn-out 'senescent' cells, and gene editing.

The key distinction researchers draw is between lifespan and healthspan: extending the number of years someone lives is very different from extending the number of healthy years. So far, no intervention has been proven to slow aging in humans.

perspectives.description: If telomerase could be activated safely, the payoff would be enormous: less suffering from cancer, heart disease and dementia, more healthy years, and lower costs for health systems worldwide. Andrews frames aging itself as the root cause of these diseases, so treating the cause rather than each illness would be a fundamentally better approach.

The main worry is cancer. Telomerase activity is a hallmark of cancer cells, which use it to divide without limit, so switching it on everywhere could give dormant tumours the tool they need. Other scientists also note that aging appears to protect the body from uncontrolled growth, and that no human trial has yet shown a telomerase-based treatment extends life.

Anti-aging promises have a long history of collapsing under scrutiny — resveratrol, telomere supplements and various 'longevity' pills were marketed long before evidence arrived. Geroscience itself makes a useful distinction between lifespan and healthspan, and serious work focuses on measured biomarkers and controlled trials rather than dramatic forecasts.

The real test is not the pill but the proof: controlled human trials, independent replication and safety data on cancer risk. If activation can be targeted to specific tissues, or paired with cancer-screening, the idea could move from claim to medicine — and then societies would still need to decide who gets access and how to pay for it.
